title: ADB: safety nets miss most poor families and are not ready for shocks
excerpt: An ADB report finds 71% of eligible families are left out of social protection, and rules stop disaster funds being released before a shock.
content:
Bangladesh's social protection system reaches about three in 10 households, citing World Bank figures, and is poorly set up to protect people from climate shocks, according to a report the Asian Development Bank (ADB) published on 18 November, Strengthening Adaptive Social Protection in Bangladesh.

The 52-page report found that 46.5% of beneficiaries did not meet the poverty criteria, while 71.0% of eligible families were excluded. Thirty-nine ministries and agencies run 115 safety net programmes, and key programmes provide less than 10.0% of the average income of poor and extremely poor households.

Social protection spending averaged 2.54% of GDP from 2015-16 to 2024-25. Without pensions and interest subsidies it was about 1.76% of GDP in 2024-25. About 10% of the 2024-25 social protection budget, over $722 million, went to disaster-related programmes.

The country faced 185 climate-related shocks from 2000 to 2019, and 58.3% of the population is exposed to climate hazards. Cyclones and floods could cost about $3.2 billion a year, about 2.2% of GDP. After Cyclone Aila in 2009, unemployment in affected south-west communities rose from 11% to 60% and the poverty headcount from 41% to 63%, the report says.

It finds that a Tk 80 billion (about $650 million) contingency fund has been little used, and that the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief's 2012 humanitarian guidelines do not allow money to be released before a shock. It recommends building adaptive social protection fully into the updated National Social Security Strategy, making anticipatory cash transfers routine, linking information systems with climate risk data, and setting up dedicated financing.

The lead authors are Shaila Rahman and Fazle Elahi Mahmud of Quay Asia, with management by Babken Babajanian of ADB. The report draws on a literature review and interviews with 26 people from government, development partners, UN agencies and civil society.

Why it matters

NGOs run much of the anticipatory cash and early recovery work in Bangladesh, often with donor money because government rules do not allow payouts before a disaster. The report backs changing those rules and fixing targeting, both of which decide who gets help when the next cyclone hits.

What to watch

Whether the updated National Social Security Strategy and the MODMR guidelines are revised to allow forecast-based transfers, and how the new Global Shield grants are linked to the safety net system.

Sources
